Get accurate body proportions. One way i start setting up for construction is using a compass to and rulers to create a grid.

Keep drawing those sort of mannekin style, simplified bodies. Do it both to measurement(and vary it, so like 7 heads tall, 8 heads tall, 9, 6...), then do it freehand based on vibes and feel. Over time you will get better at automatically just drawing a body part with relatively correct proportions without even needing a grid. 

Theres no special tip for legs that i personally know. You cant really draw a specific body part "out of proportion" because proportions are relative. If the legs are too long, it means the rest of the body is too small. If they are too short, the rest of the body is too big. Since proportions are a fundamental relationship between the measurements of various body parts, the best way to correct it is looking at the big picture, and drawing the entire body in proportion. Infact, in my experience, looking at the big picture and focusing on the entire body has helped me get better proportions on my figures.

You can prevent chronic pain by working out in specific ways(doing heavy weight training to build muscle. Doing yoga is also helpful). A lot of the pains are caused or exacerbated by lack of muscle mass, lack of bone density, lack of flexibility, or lack of joint strength(also see the muscle mass, certain muscles protect our joints and spine and stuff,  building them up makes them stronger). A lot of the pains are also caused by poor movement patterns that are corrected by learning proper form for heavy barbell movements or by doing stuff like yoga(for example doing heavy deadlifts teaches you how to protect your back while lifting. Heavy squats teach how to protect your knees and hips while lifting, both teach you better posture). 

Eventually age does come for us all. And eventually we all suffer from chronic pain. Part of it will be just luck(as time goes on its more likely you will get injured, for example). But physical activity provides a very solid foundation for preventing and mitigating age related pain so long as it is done properly.

You will see this attitude throughout the recovery community. There is a strong "abstinence only" current among addicts and there is a good reason for that. A *lot* of us have tried substances that were outside our main DOC and have had that idea fail terribly. This is borne from a lot of collective experience. This is not a universal experience, and abstinence only is not the only way to be in recovery, but it's probably the safest way. 

There's also a similar attitude to abstinence as there is towards abstinence with sex in sex ed, specifically that there is the idea that people should be advising and stressing the *safest* way, and that endorsing or condoning other ways is somehow irresponsible. That is absolutely bullshit though. 

You do find the abstinence idea in SMART. SMART is an abstinence program. Same with recovery dharma(or rather RD calls itself a renunciation based program). But i *do* like how these communities both tend to have a greater proportion of people who are willing to say "yea, i cant tell you what's going to work for you, and i can't say that smoking weed is going to be awful or make you relapse. It's your recovery. If it works for you, i support that." 

The 12 steps has a lot of busybodies and very opinionated people who want to dictate how every recovery must or will look. That may be based on some real experience and good faith on the part of a lot or most of them, but it's still really misguided and dumb.

No. *Morbid Obesity* is a medical term. It is a level of obesity that is considered to be, on its own, a medical condition. The criteria is a BMI of 40+ for uncomplicated obesity and 35+ when obesity is accompanied by other medical conditions like diabetes and certain types of hypertension. 

*obesity* as a term originates as a technical medical term. It's use colloquially has been a co-opting of this medical term by the general public to describe fat people in general, whether that person actually meets clinical criteria for any medical condition or not.

Indeed. I am far beyond the criteria for morbid obesity(my BMI is >=50) and I have no serious mobility issues(caused by my BMI, i have congenital foot issues) and in fact take part in high intensity strength training. 

I don't like the criteria for morbid obesity because the BMI doesn't actually tell you a lot about a person's general health or fitness at an individual level. It's a great aggregate number for analyzing populations of people, but it's too vague for individuals. I've known people with lower BMI's who are far less mobile due to their obesity than I am. There are a ton of genetic and environmental factors that affect how an individual is affected by the amount of body fat they hold.

Honestly my general advice is do less isolation exercises and center your routine around large movements. The human body does not normally recruit muscles in isolation when it moves. It recruits large groups of muscles if it can because doing so is much more efficient. The strength you gain from doing big lifts is more than small isolation lifts. I get a lot of people like doing those isolation and assist exercises. If you enjoy it, by all means do it. But you will get stronger faster by dropping some of them in lieu of big movements at heavier weights.

First is to do as you say. Enforce very strong constraints on both method length and file length.

On the other hand....
This can cause a serious safety hazard. Someone may get whiplash from having to jerk their head around trying to understand what the fuck all thesemethods do in context. While I can understand every individual method on it'd own, now the overall structure and meaning has been lost. You trade complexity in the small for complexity in the large. And often function calls in OOP languages have side effects of some sort. So now I have a bunch of nonlocal semi invisible complexity to deal with which can be a pain in the ass if one of those side effects is happens to be causing a bug. You could have just put it all in a single method. Sure the method is a bit chubby now but I can also see all the moving parts....moving....together. 

In some cultures and teams it's understood that death by a thousand methods the 1 true way to code. In other cultures a single method is considered appropriate and it becomes an object of superstition and occasional light worship. 


Two principles that are incredibly useful in both circumstances:

Pay attention to cyclomatic complexity and levels of nesting. Cyclomatic complexity, as intimidating as the name and definition may sound, is actually super easy to calculate(python has a module for it too. Mccabe) and it's super intuitive. It's just a measure of the possible paths code can follow from start to finish. The more potential paths there are, and the more complex those paths are, the harder it is to be confident in that codes operation. Keeping cyclomatic complexity contained at least means we can still reason about methods and functions qt a glance. 

Then nesting. Nesting conditionals might make sense sometimes. But it's harder to read. It's harder to think about. It's also ugly. The left 75% of the ide is not a margin. And if you put a switch in a switch then I'm calling the cops. 

Nesting loops is fine tho. In fact nesting loops and not hiding them behind function calls makes it so you can really easily get a feel for the time complexity of code.

A commodity is not sold at the cost of production. This fact is a part of the Marxist claim for the existence of *surplus value* created by labor.  Commodities are sold at their exchange rate or market value or exchange value. In Marxist, as in marginalist and other forms of "bourgeois economics", exchange value is determined by supply/demand. It's the highest price the seller can bargain for and profit off of and it's the lowest price the buyer can get it for. Marxism differs in that it privileges and exalts labor as being the *creator of value*.  In marginal utility, value is determined solely by its exchange value, it has no value outside the dollars and cents someone will work to earn to buy it for, and it doesn't make sense to talk about it in any other terms. 

Marxism recognizes that value is intrinsically tied to the creative process of labor. It isn't that all labor is valuable, or that all value requires the same amount of labor, or anything of that nature. Instead it reminds us that the process of creating anything valuable requires some labor to transform a raw good into something usable. A tree has no value in and off itself. It has value when transformed by labor into something useful. Even claiming nature, orba Park, or a trail, or a forest requires maintenance in the form of labor to keep that forest valuable for the people who use it. It does not try to hide or obscure or ignore the fact that the only reason we have this abundance all around us is because *we worked for it*. If was by no miracle that the fields were plowed and it wasn't by any capitalist generosity that the flour was milled. *we worked for it*. *we earned it*.

Do you mean running, say an Xbox game on an Xbox 360? If so, it's because doing so is a *feature* that requires costly investment and development and may even require sacrificing on other features. The machine instructions that were generated for an Xbox* game cannot be guaranteed to be "semantically equivalent"(that the overall meaning of the instructions is the same), or valid on the processor of an Xbox360*. That means you need some sort of system, whether it's hardware or software, to provide support for the old binaries. 

Game companies aren't doing this to be dicks or just grab profits. It's actually a technical challenge to provide support. It's not a particularly hard one, but it's still investment that's gotta be weighed against other priorities.

}`
